[84] The Government's Security and Emergency Preparedness Policy

[85] Norway is a long country, but there are strong ties that unite us

[86] We have settlements throughout the country and fundamental trust in each other and in the authorities

[87] The society of trust and safe, good and vibrant local communities throughout the country are the most important building blocks of Norwegian civil preparedness

[88] Different parts of the country and different groups in society may have different emergency preparedness challenges

[89] No matter where you live in Norway or who you are, the community should stand up when it is really needed

[90] With this announcement, the government is pointing a completely new direction in the development of total preparedness throughout the country to strengthen the resilience of the entire population

[91] The need for a new security and emergency preparedness policy Norway finds itself in a more dangerous and unpredictable world

[92] The serious security situation in Europe as a result of Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine, the war in the Middle East, and heightened global competition and rivalry between great powers such as the United States and China for military, political, economic and technological power characterize our time

[93] Technological developments challenge security and preparedness in ways we cannot fully foresee

[94] The digitalization of society, the use of social media, and the development of new technology such as artificial intelligence contribute to this

[95] Climate change increases the risk of natural hazards here at home, and can lead to strong migration and conflicts globally

[96] In the face of this societal development, Norway must strengthen its overall defense capability

[97] The government's long-term plan for the defense sector is a significant boost to our military capability

[98] The government is now presenting a historic total preparedness announcement

[99] In the report, the government sets the direction for a restructuring of the civilian part of the total defense and for the civilian resistance force

[100] We must ensure that civil society is prepared for crisis and war, and develop a society that supports military efforts and resists complex threats

[101] This includes planning to meet acts of war on Norwegian territory as well as on allied territory

[102] Russia's willingness to use military force to achieve political goals shows that Norway will likely have to deal with an unpredictable and risk-taking neighbor for a long time to come

[103] China's closer strategic partnership with Russia and support for the war in Ukraine are disturbing, while we depend on cooperation with China in certain areas to solve the greatest challenges of our time

[104] The combined use of instruments makes the distinction between peace and crisis less clear, and challenges the traditional distinction between state security and societal security

[105] Disinformation, influence operations, covert investments in strategic business activities, disruptions in supply chains, insiders in private or public companies, and more frequent digital attacks have become a common part of the threat landscape

[106] Combined use of drugs often continues over a long period of time and includes both legal and illegal drugs

[107] The activity often takes place covertly through the use of intermediaries, and increasingly, state actors use profit-motivated criminals to carry out operations

[108] The activity can be challenging to understand, detect, handle and counteract, and it affects us all

[109] See further discussion in chapter

[110] The population's ability to distinguish between truth and falsehood is being challenged

[111] Threats may be intended to create discord between groups and destabilize society

[112] The business sector owns much of society's critical infrastructure and is central to important value chains, and is vulnerable to digital attacks, insiders and intelligence leaks

[113] Foreign actors may wish to disrupt basic services to the population and thereby weaken society's resilience

[114] Municipalities must ensure safety in local communities and constitute an important part of the country's basic preparedness

[115] Crisis and war could challenge municipalities' ability to maintain basic services for the population

[116] This development and the complexity of the threat landscape require a more vigilant and more resilient civil society

[117] Population, voluntary 12 Report

[118] Parliament 2024–

[119] Organizations, private businesses, and local, regional, and state authorities must increasingly recognize that security and preparedness are something we must all take responsibility for and contribute to

[120] The Government will ensure that society's collective resources are better utilized in both preventing and handling crises, and ensure close involvement of the private sector and volunteers

[121] During any event high on the crisis spectrum, it is necessary for society to have the prerequisites and a culture of preparedness to be able to handle various incidents and crises

[122] Greater demands are placed on the population's own preparedness

[123] The increasingly close link between the economy and security means that the business community must increasingly integrate national security considerations into its decisions

[124] Municipalities must systematically plan for major events where society depends on resources finding each other

[125] Businesses, municipalities and county governments must be able to make good assessments to safeguard national security

[126] Strengthening society's resilience in the face of this development requires a wide range of measures: regulation, financing, guidance, collaboration and self-preparedness

[127] The sum of measures at various levels will contribute to awareness, knowledge and shared understanding of the situation, and make us better prepared as a society

[128] At the same time, we cannot fully protect society from all threats

[129] Events will occur

[130] Which measures to implement must be based on an assessment of risk, and which risks we must accept and live with

[131] We must know what interests and values we should protect

[132] In emergency preparedness work, long-term thinking is important

[133] Therefore, the government set up a total emergency preparedness commission in January

[134] The Commission has assessed the strengths and weaknesses of current emergency preparedness systems, and proposed how society's overall resources can and should be directed to further develop resilience and ensure the best possible overall utilization of emergency preparedness resources

[135] Recommendations from the Total Emergency Preparedness Commission's report NOU

[137] Prerequisites for a new security and emergency preparedness policy

[138] Emergency preparedness policy must be based on our strategic interests and exploit our advantages

[139] At the same time, the efforts must be based on an understanding of the vulnerabilities we face

[140] Norway is a resource-rich country, with a knowledgeable population and a society characterized by trust in each other and in the authorities

[141] The business community, the social partners and public authorities are used to working together

[142] We must build and preserve a society where people and resources throughout the country find each other in both preventing and managing crises

[143] Economic resilience is a pillar of Norwegian society

[144] A well-functioning economy, trade and financial stability are prerequisites for maintaining the basic functionality of society

[145] Norway has an open economy that has extensive trade with the outside world

[146] Cooperation and interaction with other countries is important

[147] Norway is a significant export nation

[148] We also have significant imports

[149] During the pandemic, we saw how international cooperation was important for access to vaccines

[150] At the same time, in the face of today's threat, we must strengthen national control over critical infrastructure, natural resources, property, and strategically important businesses and value chains

[151] The High North is our most important strategic area and of great importance in today's security political situation

[152] Our room for maneuver in the area is being challenged by Russia

[153] At the same time, China is showing increasing interest in the region

[154] Norway is a significant energy nation

[155] After the war in Ukraine, Norwegian energy supplies to Europe have taken on even greater security policy significance

[156] This makes us vulnerable to pressure and sabotage actions throughout the value chain

[157] With one of the world's longest coastlines, we are particularly vulnerable to maritime covert intelligence activity

[158] This challenges, among other things, our maritime industry and critical infrastructure

[159] Norway is a highly digitalized society

[160] It is important for our competitiveness and innovative power, but at the same time it brings with it vulnerabilities with great potential for harm to society

[161] Norway is well anchored in a Western and European community of values ​​and interests

[162] NATO is the cornerstone of Norwegian security policy and crucial for our defense capability

[163] Finnish and Swedish NATO membership means new opportunities for strengthened Nordic cooperation, also within security and preparedness

[164] In Europe, Norway has its most important trading partners, and several important collaborations within civil emergency preparedness have been established

[165] This international community is crucial for Norway's security, but is increasingly challenged by actors who want to create discord and weaken society in Western countries

[166] Total preparedness report 1.3 The Government's goals and priorities

[167] The background to this message is the most serious security situation in Europe since World War II

[168] Through the long-term plan for the defense sector, the government and the Storting have jointly adopted a historic strengthening of Norway's defense

[169] The challenges we face as a society also make it necessary to strengthen civil preparedness

[170] Ever since World War II, the defense of Norway has been based on the total defense concept

[171] The concept is a recognition that support and cooperation between civilian and military resources helps Norway to counter and manage threats to society and the state

[172] On the civilian side, we must first and foremost make better use of society's overall resources

[173] State and local authorities, business and voluntary sectors must collaborate more closely so that resources find each other more quickly when a crisis occurs

[174] Civil society must make plans that harmonize with military planning, and prioritize resources where they are needed most

[175] Civilian authorities, the Armed Forces, private businesses and volunteers must have a common situational understanding and train more together

[176] In light of the current security policy situation, this report emphasizes the work on total defense and civil society's resilience in situations where the worst-case scenario were to happen, and Norway were to once again experience armed conflict or war

[177] The Norwegian preparedness model is also based on the fact that the resources in the total defense also have tasks in everyday preparedness in the event of natural disasters, major accidents and other serious incidents

[178] When we now strengthen preparedness for the upper crisis spectrum, it will also contribute to strengthening society's ability to prevent and handle other incidents

[179] Only through a resilient and enduring civil society can Norway resist a more acute and complicated threat landscape

[180] Three main goals underpin the government's work to strengthen civil society's resilience

[181] A civil society that is prepared for crisis and war A civil society that resists complex threats

[182] A civil society that supports military efforts

[183] In this message, the government presents a number of measures that strengthen civil society's resilience and contribute to achieving the government's main goals

[184] These measures are based on seven strategic directions for the government's work, see box

[185] Ensuring settlement and activity in local communities throughout the country Settlement, activity and vibrant local communities throughout the country are of crucial importance for Norway

[186] The Government will therefore pursue a comprehensive policy that ensures settlement throughout the country, so that we can maintain a vibrant and sustainable society

[187] The Government will ensure solid local communities and good local emergency preparedness

[188] Ensure good basic preparedness in local communities Prevention and good basic preparedness help ensure that crises can be handled as quickly as possible locally

[189] The municipalities have a crucial role in preventive work and in incident management

[190] The government's proposal that all municipalities should have or be affiliated with a municipal emergency preparedness council will contribute to strengthened preventive work, and to Box

[191] Seven strategic priorities for the government's work on security and preparedness The government shall: Ensure settlement, good basic preparedness and vibrant local communities throughout the country

[192] Make better use of society's overall resources in prevention and crisis management, including involving businesses and volunteers in emergency preparedness work locally, regionally and nationally

[193] Strengthen digital resilience and national control over critical infrastructure and strategically important businesses, natural resources, property and assets

[194] Strengthen the resilience of the population and maintain a high level of trust in society

[195] Strengthen security of supply, including food security

[196] Ensure closer cooperation between civilian sectors and the defense sector

[197] Strengthen civilian capacity to support allied military efforts within the framework of NATO and through strengthened Nordic and European emergency preparedness cooperation

[218] Increase support for voluntary organizations

[219] The voluntary organizations in the rescue service are a central part of basic preparedness in Norway

[220] The government will facilitate an increase in subsidies for volunteers in the rescue service by up to NOK 100 million through an escalation over eight years

[223] Utilize society's collective resources better in prevention and crisis management, including involving businesses and volunteers in emergency preparedness work locally, regionally and nationally. All civilian sectors must be prepared for serious crises and war

[224] To ensure good information sharing and the most efficient and flexible utilization of society's overall resources, better coordination and prioritization of resources between the public sector, business and voluntary sectors is necessary

[226] Establish a new council structure with requirements for the involvement of private business and volunteers. The Government will establish a unified council structure at national, regional and local levels to strengthen the coordination of emergency preparedness work

[227] At the national level, emergency response councils will be established within critical areas of society where such councils do not exist today

[228] The councils shall be led by the responsible ministry, and have participation from other public actors, the business community and the voluntary sector

[238] The new council structure for emergency planning and condition assessments in civilian sectors provides the government with a good basis for preparing the long-term plan

[240] Promote proposals for a new law on basic security of socially important businesses

[241] The government will propose a new law on basic security for socially important businesses

[242] The Act should be seen in the context of the work to prepare the implementation of the directives on security of network and information systems (NIS2 Directive) and the resilience of critical entities (CER Directive

[243] The new law will set common requirements for basic security in businesses that are important for the functioning of society, in peace, crisis and war

[244] Strengthening common situational awareness against complex threats In order to prevent, resist and manage complex threats, it is crucial that we as a society understand what we are facing and what values we possess

[245] The National Intelligence and Security Centre (NESS) consists of the Police Security Service, the Intelligence Service, the National Security Authority and the police

[246] The center works to strengthen the national ability to detect complex threats and ensure good decision-making support for the authorities

[247] The Ministry of Justice and Emergency Preparedness and the Ministry of Defence are now further developing NESS to establish a national situational picture against complex threats, and to strengthen the cross-sectoral work necessary to detect, understand, counter and manage the use of complex means

[366] The comprehensive preparedness report The broad preparedness work and comprehensive defense

[367] This White Paper emphasizes resistance power and total defense in situations high on the crisis spectrum, that is, our ability to prevent and handle complex threats, security policy crises, armed conflict and, in the worst case, war

[368] These are situations that arise as a result of intentional actions by one or more threat actors, and where they have the intention to harm us

[369] The perspective in the report is motivated by the security policy situation

[370] However, the work on resilience and preparedness has a much broader scope

[371] The broad emergency preparedness work is aimed at preventing and handling a range of different incidents, all of which can have serious consequences

[372] There can be serious natural events such as extreme weather

[373] Hans" in 2023 (see box 2.1) and quicksand landslide at Gjerdrum in 2020 (see box 2.2), accidents like the one with the cruise ship

[374] Viking cloud" outside Hustadsvika in 2019 (see box 2.3), or intentional actions that have serious consequences, such as a computer attack

[375] Strengthening broad emergency preparedness work ensures basic preparedness in society

[376] The work on broad preparedness, including good collaboration, is also important for our ability to handle incidents high on the crisis spectrum, because it will largely be the same actors and resources that we also use in handling the most serious incidents

[377] Extreme weather "Hans" In August 2023, extreme weather Hans hit southern Norway

[378] It led to landslides, flash floods, floods and inundations

[379] An unusually severe weather system with very heavy rainfall came on top of an already high groundwater level after heavy rain in late summer and early fall

[380] Damage to infrastructure and property was extensive

[381] The consequences continued for several weeks after the storm was over

[382] The evaluation of the incident management concluded that the extreme weather event Hans was generally handled very well

[383] Early and good notification between the various actors was crucial for good and coordinated handling

[384] The resources from the various central, regional and local actors found each other, and actors such as the Home Guard, the Civil Defence, voluntary organisations (such as the Red Cross, Norwegian People's Aid and the Norwegian Women's Sanitary Association), as well as private actors and the business sector, were important in handling the incident

[385] The evaluation comes with several recommendations to further strengthen preparedness

[386] These include, among other things, the need for better guidance for municipalities in systematic work on flood and landslide protection, for municipalities to conduct more exercises based on their own needs and analyses, and for the Norwegian Meteorological Institute and the Norwegian Water Resources and Energy Directorate to provide earlier, clearer and more consequence-based warnings of extreme weather, so that relevant actors have even more time to prepare

[387] The evaluation has contributed to a good knowledge base for handling future extreme weather events

[388] Actors affected by the recommendations are preparing plans for their own follow-up

[389] Evaluation of the extreme weather event Hans – prevention, preparedness and management

[410] On March 2019, the cruise ship Viking Sky experienced engine failure and was in distress at Hustadvika between Kristiansund and Molde

[411] The ship was very close to running aground, which could have had catastrophic consequences

[412] An extensive rescue effort was initiated and almost 500 passengers were evacuated by helicopter and transported to a reception center on land

[413] The evaluation of the incident establishes that the rescue operation was successful, with very good efforts and good cooperation between the actors involved

[414] Subsequently, a public committee was appointed to assess the emergency preparedness challenges associated with increasing cruise traffic in Norwegian waters

[415] A public report was submitted to the Minister of Justice and Public Security in 2022 (NOU

[416] The report made a number of recommendations, with a primary emphasis on risk-reducing measures

[418] A number of the recommendations have been followed up through ongoing emergency preparedness work in a number of businesses

[420] The reviews also show the breadth of actors involved in handling such incidents

[421] In addition to public agencies at central and regional level and in affected municipalities, a number of voluntary organizations and many private businesses participated in the rescue operation

[444] The four basic principles for work on civil protection – The principle of responsibility means that the organization that is responsible for a subject area in a normal situation is also responsible for the necessary emergency preparedness preparations and for handling extraordinary incidents in the area

[445] The responsible body must decide what is an acceptable risk. – The principle of similarity means that the organization you operate with during crises should initially be as similar as possible to the organization you have on a daily basis

[446] – The subsidiarity principle means that crises should be handled organizationally at the lowest possible level

[447] – The principle of cooperation means that authorities, businesses or agencies have an independent responsibility to ensure the best possible cooperation with relevant actors and businesses in the work of prevention, preparedness and crisis management

[658] The total preparedness report for the crisis spectrum is based on civil-military cooperation, and cooperation with and involvement of private actors and volunteers, largely on partnerships, voluntary arrangements or binding agreements

[659] The Armed Forces are today a significant and important emergency preparedness actor for civilian society in peacetime

[660] The Armed Forces assist in handling a number of different incidents, such as floods, landslides, various accidents and in handling extraordinary events such as the coronavirus pandemic

[661] The Armed Forces also have a role in terrorism preparedness

[662] The Armed Forces also contribute with certain regular tasks in the day-to-day life of the civilian side

[663] Examples are the Rescue Helicopter Service, the Border Guard and the Coast Guard, which, among other things, carry out fisheries and catch supervision, towing readiness, customs supervision, environmental protection tasks, etc

[664] In addition, the Armed Forces carry out a number of tasks upon request, to support the police or other public authorities and emergency response actors responsible for public safety, critical societal functions or critical infrastructure, etc

[665] In situations at the top of the crisis spectrum, society's resource use, priorities and task solutions will change significantly

[666] First, For the answer will have to prioritize its sizing

[667] duties, and the Armed Forces' assistance to the civilian side could be downgraded and may be discontinued altogether

[668] At the same time, in such situations, the Armed Forces will be able to seize civilian operational resources, such as rescue helicopters, etc

[669] These will then have reduced capacity to handle tasks in civilian sectors

[670] The Armed Forces will also increase staffing by mobilizing the Home Guard and reservists in the rest of the Armed Forces structure

[671] This means that many people are pulled out of their daily tasks and civilian jobs

[672] Other resources could also be clearly affected

[673] For example, railway transport capacity may be tied up in the transport of military equipment and personnel, health and care services may have to use significant resources to treat injured military personnel, and courts may have to use significant resources to handle cases related to

[674] to war The Norwegian total defense concept

[675] The Norwegian total defense concept was developed in the period after World War II

[676] The Defence Commission of 1946 emphasized in its report the importance of strengthening the Armed Forces through a total defence concept

[677] The defense of Norway should be based on both military defense and broad civil preparedness

[678] The goal was, and still is, both to protect Norway's territory, independence and national values, and to protect the civilian population

[679] However, the focus of the total defense concept has changed over time

[680] During the Cold War, the focus of the concept was essentially in line with the Defence Commission's recommendation of 1946, i.e. how the civilian sector should support the Defence Forces (war capability) in armed conflict while maintaining a minimum of the basic functionality of civil society and the basic security of the population

[681] After the Cold War, the focus shifted to how the Armed Forces, as a significant peacetime emergency resource, can support civil society to ensure good preparedness and the best possible utilization of society's overall resources to solve missions lower on the crisis spectrum

[682] This distortion meant, among other things, that several of the measures aimed at situations involving war, the threat of war or similar conditions (so called war planning within civil emergency preparedness work) were discontinued throughout the 1990s and early 2000s

[683] An example of this is that there has been an exemption from building shelters in new buildings after the current total defense concept was adopted through the Storting's consideration of the modernization of the Armed Forces

[688] S. no. 49 (2004–2005), and encompasses mutual support and cooperation between the Armed Forces and civil society in connection with prevention, emergency planning, crisis management and consequence management across the entire crisis spectrum from peace via security policy crises to armed conflict

[689] Civilian support for military efforts at the upper end of the crisis spectrum (the original purpose) has gradually gained greater focus in recent years, and particularly after Russia's war against Ukraine in 2014 (Donbas in eastern Ukraine and Crimea

[691] Offers to civilians and capacity to carry out ordinary tasks may be reduced

[692] Civil society must therefore be prepared to handle serious incidents itself to a much greater extent

[693] Without assistance from the Armed Forces, the consequences of unwanted incidents could be more serious than they would be in a normal situation

[694] The use of civilian resources to support military efforts can therefore be a double-edged sword

[695] If civil society is unable to take care of itself, and thus also unable to support military efforts, the deterrent effect of a resilient society could also decrease

[696] On the other hand, without sufficient support for the military defense of Norway, there will be nothing left to defend

[697] In situations higher up the crisis spectrum, it becomes more legitimate and relevant to take measures that can be very intrusive and that are not authorized to be used in situations lower on the crisis spectrum

[698] A large part of the emergency preparedness regulations has a situational requirement that we must be high on the crisis spectrum before the regulations can be applied

[699] Examples may include, in addition to mobilizing the Armed Forces through conscription, curfews to reduce the burden on emergency services, for example, rationing of goods such as fuel and electricity, and the discharge of civilian labor

[700] The requisitioning, expropriation, internment, forced relocation of people are other examples

[701] More intrusive measures, and an increased emphasis on the Armed Forces' dimensioning tasks, are based on specific assessments of the seriousness and scope of the situation, and that the decisions made are necessary and proportionate

[702] Events high on the crisis spectrum will likely affect different parts of the country differently

[703] In some geographical areas, residents will be able to live almost as normal, with more normal access to public services, shops, etc., while other areas will be heavily affected by war with a corresponding reduction in private and public services

[704] Nevertheless, less directly affected areas will also be affected, for example by prioritizing personnel and other resources to support the military effort, and by public authorities focusing their attention on the ongoing incident, or by the arrival of internally displaced persons from the affected area

[705] A civil society in a situation high on the crisis spectrum will therefore be very different from that in peacetime

[706] It will affect citizens, businesses, organizations and society

[707] The better we are prepared for this, the better we will handle the most demanding situations

[708] This also emphasizes the importance of trust

[709] Norway is a country with a high level of trust between the population and the authorities, between public and private actors, and between different groups in society

[710] Reduced trust between groups in society creates vulnerabilities that threat actors can exploit to further weaken trust and ultimately undermine democracy

[711] Therefore, we must continuously work to maintain the level of trust, including through good and informed public discourse about the challenges we face and current measures

[712] High on the crisis spectrum – prepared for war

[714] There is a wide range of possible incidents, and the severity and consequences of a given type of incident, such as a computer attack or a forest fire, can vary significantly

[715] At the top of the crisis spectrum we find armed conflict and war, i.e. situations where state security is threatened

[716] Composite threats are a significant part of today's threat landscape

[840] Long-term plan for civil preparedness

[841] The government will prepare a long-term plan for civil preparedness

[842] The Total Emergency Preparedness Commission recommends that a long-term plan for civil preparedness be established

[843] The Commission emphasizes that today's challenging situation increases the need to strengthen preparedness across sectors, and that it is important to have mechanisms that support comprehensive assessments

[844] The Commission also underlines that the work on a long-term plan for civil preparedness must be seen in the context of the work on a new long-term plan for the defence sector

[845] The government has taken several powerful steps to strengthen preparedness

[846] With the new long-term plan for the defense sector, the government has laid the foundation for a significant and long-term strengthening of Norway's defense capabilities

[847] In this report, the government lays the foundation for a significant strengthening of civil preparedness in the short and long term

[848] The government will present a national security strategy in the spring of 2025 that will support efforts to safeguard national security interests

[849] The government nevertheless agrees with the Total Emergency Preparedness Commission that there is a need for more long-term planning on the civil side, and will therefore create a long-term plan for civil emergency preparedness

[850] The plan will facilitate more long-term and holistic management, prioritization, planning and development of central preparedness resources on the civilian side

[851] The design of the plan must take into account that there are differences between long-term planning in the defense sector and on the civilian side

[852] While the long-term plan for the defense sector deals with one sector and one level of administration, civil preparedness is cross-sectoral, encompassing all levels of administration, the business community and the voluntary sector

[853] The business community owns and operates critical infrastructure, including electronic communications, energy and financial services

[854] Volunteering plays a central role in preparedness throughout the country

[855] The sectors that are part of civil emergency preparedness have different areas of responsibility and are organized differently

[856] They encompass everything from healthcare and space technology to the grocery industry

[857] The fewest actors have preparedness as their main concern, but are primarily engaged in the production of goods and services

[858] This must be taken into account when planning emergency preparedness efforts

[859] In many sectors, the work of understanding threats, assessing preventive measures, practicing incident management, and establishing new knowledge is just as important as considering larger long-term investments

[860] The long-term plan for civil preparedness must therefore have a different structure than the long-term plan for the defense sector

[861] Work on the long-term plan for civil preparedness will begin in 2025 with the establishment of the new council structure for emergency planning and situation assessments in civil sectors, see section 3.1. The Government aims to have emergency preparedness councils in all critical areas of society by

[864] The plan must address the need for long-term, cross-sectoral planning, but at the same time take into account the specific features of the civil emergency preparedness field and be sufficiently flexible to meet a constantly changing threat and challenge picture

[865] The purpose of the long-term plan is to strengthen civil preparedness, ensure continuity, coordination and long-term thinking

[866] The long-term plan will strengthen the link between risk assessments and policy measures

[867] The long-term plan will be a tool for assessing future staffing needs compared to the staffing needs in society as a whole

[868] The long-term planning work will be based on documents that describe the challenges, threats and risks, for example the national security strategy, see section 3.4, worst-case scenarios from the Directorate for Civil Protection and Emergency Preparedness, risk assessments from the National Security Authority, and police advice from the Police Directorate

[915] National Security Strategy

[916] The government has initiated work on a national security strategy

[917] A national security strategy is a cross-sectoral document that provides a comprehensive framework for how a state should promote its own security interests in the face of its environment and threats

[918] Key allies such as the United States and Britain have had variations of such strategies over time

[919] Germany presented its first national security strategy in 2023, as part of the response to Russia's war of aggression in Ukraine

[920] Sweden presented the second edition of its security strategy this summer

[921] Norway has not previously had a national security strategy

[922] In 2023, the government received input from the Defence Commission, the Total Emergency Preparedness Commission and the National Security Authority's Security Expert Council, all of which point to the need for such a strategy

[923] Common to all the inputs is that the seriousness of the times we live in, the breadth of security challenges and changes in the framework conditions for Norwegian security reinforce the need for more coordination, comprehensiveness and long-termism in Norway's security, defence and emergency preparedness arrangements

[924] The inputs have been considered in the usual way by relevant ministries and the Prime Minister's Office

[925] In June 2024, the Storting passed a unanimous resolution asking the government to develop a national security strategy

[926] This is a mission the government takes seriously

[927] There are various documents that present important considerations, goals and priorities of importance for security work, such as reports to the Storting on societal security, long-term plans for the defense sector, and, among other things, strategies for digital security, artificial intelligence and counterterrorism work

[928] The Government will prepare a national security strategy that provides a comprehensive, overarching presentation of foreign, security, defense and emergency preparedness policies, based on our national security

[929] The strategy will be based on the following principles

[930] underlying national values and interests, and how these should be promoted and defended over time

[931] To ensure that the affected policy areas are seen together, and to emphasize the central position of the strategy, the Prime Minister's Office will act as the issuer of the strategy

[986] Involvement of private industry

[987] It is important that we have a diverse business sector throughout the country

[988] Private business owns, operates and develops critical infrastructure, and plays a crucial role both in our ability to ensure continuity of critical societal functions and in civilian support for military operations

[989] They have important knowledge about how technical systems are built, potential vulnerabilities in them, and how any damage and downtime can be handled

[990] The business community, including industrial safety, has a number of tangible resources, such as personnel and mechanical equipment, which can be of great use in handling incidents

[991] Businesses also have a vested interest in being able to prevent and handle demanding events that affect them, since disruptions in the production of goods and services can be costly and ultimately lead to bankruptcy

[992] Many risk-reducing measures are therefore profitable from both a business and socio-economic perspective

[993] Private business therefore has an important role across the entire spectrum of crises, both towards the civilian population and in supporting the defense effort

[994] Increased involvement and collaboration with the private sector With this announcement, the government strengthens and formalizes involvement and collaboration with the private sector on security and emergency preparedness

[995] This happens through two main tracks

[996] Firstly, the participation of private and voluntary organisations in the new structure for condition assessments and preparedness is formalised. Industrial safety is industry's own emergency response that can quickly handle fires, personal injuries and leaks of gas and hazardous chemicals before the emergency services arrive

[997] Industrial safety is a statutory requirement for self-protection that applies to most large and medium-sized industrial enterprises

[998] Businesses that fall under regulations on industrial safety are obliged to establish industrial safety

[999] When it is deemed necessary based on an enterprise's risk or location, the Norwegian Business Safety Organization may require enterprises other than those initially covered by the regulations to establish industrial safety

[1000] Businesses subject to industrial safety obligations must conduct a risk assessment and identify which undesirable incidents may occur at their premises

[1001] This determines how they will organize, equip and practice their industrial safety

[1081] NATO – the cornerstone of Norwegian security policy NATO's security guarantee and ability to respond collectively are crucial to our defense capability

[1082] Civilian counter-terrorism is essential for the Alliance's collective response and for credible deterrence

[1083] The Alliance's work on both civil resilience and military capability at the national and allied levels is anchored in Article 3 of the NATO Treaty

[1084] In order to achieve more effectively the purposes of this Treaty, the Parties will individually and jointly, by constant and effective self-help and mutual support, maintain and develop their individual and collective capacity to resist armed attack

[1085] NATO has three core civil preparedness functions

[1086] i) to maintain state governance and crisis management, ii) to maintain basic services to the population, and iii) to support military efforts

[1087] Based on these three core functions, NATO member states have adopted seven basic expectations for resilience in critical civil society functions and formulated further criteria for these in the form of resilience goals

[1088] It is up to each individual ally to operationalize the common goals for civilian sectors and develop national implementation plans

[1089] All member states must report on implementation to NATO

[1090] The goals point to several relevant civilian (public and private) areas that are important to include in allied countries' national work

[1184] Box 3.10 Norwegian civilian support to Ukraine

[1185] Since the outbreak of the war, Ukraine has submitted over 200 formal requests for assistance for civilian support through the EU Civil Protection Mechanism, EU Civil Protection Mechanism

[1186] The Directorate for Civil Protection and Emergency Preparedness is the national contact point for reception and response to assistance needs within the scheme

[1187] By virtue of their coordination role, the directorate shall ensure interaction with relevant agencies during international incidents, a role that has been an important prerequisite for Norwegian civilian support to Ukraine through UCPM

[1188] Norwegian authorities have chosen the EU Civil Emergency Mechanism as a main channel for providing civilian humanitarian assistance to Ukraine, partly because the EU Crisis Management Centre was early in establishing a stable logistics apparatus for delivering assistance to Ukraine

[1189] A clear experience is that the war has cross-sectoral impacts

[1190] As of October 2024, 26 different Ukrainian authorities have requested assistance through the EU's Civil Emergency Response Mechanism, and Norway has provided materials to the Ukrainian health sector and to civil emergency authorities for the protection of the population

[1191] Norway has also supplied materials for the protection of Ukrainian cultural heritage, as well as materials for the reconstruction of critical infrastructure in Ukraine

[1192] When Russia launched a full-scale attack on Ukraine, there was an urgent need for medical evacuation of Ukrainian patients

[1193] The EU quickly put in place a mechanism to handle the need, and the first evacuation to Norway took place in March

[1194] To date, Norway has received more than 400 Ukrainian patients through the EU's civil preparedness mechanism

[1195] Since August 2022, Norway has collaborated with the EU on regular evacuation flights for Ukrainian patients, transporting more than 2,000 patients to life-saving healthcare in Norway and other European countries

[1196] In this way, we contribute to utilizing hospital capacity in several countries to relieve the burden on Ukraine's healthcare system

[1197] Norway is the only country offering regular flights through the EU's civil protection scheme, and the cooperation agreement on the regular flights runs until April

[1198] The Norwegian civil-military cooperation that underlies our contribution to the medical evacuation of Ukrainian patients has accounted for almost half of all flights to European countries

[1199] Norwegian expertise is referred to as a pillar of the joint European effort for the medical evacuation of Ukrainian patients

[1202] Increased ability for crisis management

[1203] Our ability to handle crises is of great importance for the extent of the consequences that incidents have on life, health and material assets

[1204] We must be able to make decisions, build situational understanding, acquire necessary expertise and share information

[1205] When an incident occurs, it usually affects multiple sectors

[1206] Serious incidents and crises have cross-sectoral consequences

[1207] There may be a need for coordination between the defense sector and civilian sectors, between sectors on the civilian side, between different levels of administration, and between the public sector and private and voluntary actors

[1208] When handling incidents high on the crisis spectrum, there will be a particular need for routines, instructions and legislation for coordination to be clear, binding and well known

[1209] These also need to be practiced regularly

[1210] Although the current system for crisis management works well, experiences from, among other things, the ongoing war in Ukraine, the corona pandemic, the incident with the cruise ship "Viking Sky" in 2019 and the extreme weather "Hans" in 2023 have highlighted a need for clear roles, responsibilities and authority

[1215] • involve and collaborate more closely with the business community in exercises

[1216] • conduct a new national exercise for digital security

[1217] • contribute to increased access to unclassified and classified communication solutions for relevant civilian activities in the total defense

[1218] • ensure the development of a new emergency network that meets the need for coverage, national control, security and technological development

[1222] that the state takes over ownership and management of the part of the coastal radio service that is defined as a special socially imposed task when the agreement with Telenor expires on December

[1305] The Ministry of Justice and Public Security as the permanent lead ministry in civil national crises

[1306] According to the Civil Security Instructions, the Ministry of Justice and Public Security is the permanent lead ministry in civil national crises unless otherwise determined

[1307] The lead ministry shall coordinate and coordinate the handling of crises at the ministry level

[1308] The appointment of a lead ministry does not entail changes in constitutional responsibilities, and all ministries retain responsibility and decision-making authority for their respective areas of expertise

[1309] Experience shows that incidents will often require one ministry to coordinate the handling across sectors

[1310] This applies regardless of whether the incident is defined as a national crisis or not, because the distinction between crises and other serious incidents is not clear-cut

[1311] At the same time, the Ministry of Justice and Public Security has a general coordination role within public security work

[1312] This role means that the Ministry of Justice and Public Security is responsible for comprehensive, systematic and risk-based work on societal security at the national level across all sectors, including ensuring that issues across sectors and critical societal functions are handled, and, if necessary, assisting ministries in clarifying responsibilities

[1313] The coordination role and the lead ministry role largely require the same type of expertise, regardless of whether the incident is a crisis or not

[1314] It is therefore natural that both roles are handled by the same ministry

[1315] A ministry that has rarely or never previously held the role of lead ministry will not have the same qualifications as the Ministry of Justice and Public Security to fulfill this role

[1316] The government will therefore

[1480] These services are largely based on global navigation satellite systems (GNSS), the most well-known of which is GPS

[1481] The use of GPS has revolutionized many aspects of our modern society, but GPS signals are vulnerable to jamming

[1482] Jamming is the interference or blocking of, among other things, GPS signals

[1483] Outages and disruptions of GNSS signals could result in major economic consequences for society, or loss of life and health

[1484] According to the Norwegian Communications Authority, in 2020 a total of 20 days with GPS signal outages were reported in Eastern Finnmark, in 2022 the number had increased to 120 days, and in 2023 there were outages almost daily

[1485] An annual jam test is held on Andøya, with several hundred participants from all over the world

[1486] The jamming test is the world's largest open civilian jamming test, and has become a unique and important collaborative arena where authorities and industry players from Norway and abroad can together test their systems and expose them to real and realistic interference

[1487] The jamming tests help make systems more robust and secure against GNSS interference

[1609] Strengthen the municipality's emergency preparedness work

[1610] Municipalities are a foundation and an important interdisciplinary coordination arena in the national preparedness

[1611] Municipalities are important in ensuring the safety of the population, both through the services they provide on a daily basis, but also through the preparedness they must have to handle crises

[1612] Obligation regarding municipal emergency response councils

[1613] Municipalities have extensive emergency preparedness responsibility across the entire crisis spectrum

[1614] Key activities in the municipality include work on comprehensive risk and vulnerability analyses, an overall emergency preparedness plan, exercises and crisis management

[1615] The municipalities' emergency preparedness responsibilities are regulated, among other things, through the Act on Municipal Emergency Preparedness Obligation, Civil Protection Measures and the Civil Defence (Civil Protection Act), and in the Health and Social Preparedness Act (Health Preparedness Act) and associated regulations

[1616] Municipalities are also subject to the Security Act

[1617] In addition, municipalities are planning authorities, which is of great importance in the work of preventing the consequences of future climate-related events

[1618] Municipal emergency preparedness councils are important for the municipalities' coordination and leadership roles in security and emergency preparedness work

[1619] Emergency preparedness councils often consist of local actors from both political and administrative leadership in the municipality, representatives from the voluntary sector, business, and public actors such as the police, the Civil Defence and the Armed Forces

[1620] The emergency preparedness councils are an important arena for mutual exchange of information, discussion and coordination of emergency preparedness work in the municipality

[1621] The advice is also important for sharing situational awareness at the local level

[1622] This can improve the quality of municipalities' reporting to the state administrator

[1623] However, the emergency councils do not have decision-making authority

[1624] It is the individual agency and municipality that exercises the authority granted to them

[1625] It is not currently a requirement for municipalities to have, or be affiliated with, an emergency preparedness council

[1626] The state administrators, in turn, are obliged to have a county emergency council with detailed requirements for participation and what role the council should play

[1627] The municipal survey for 2024 shows that nationwide, 75% of municipalities have established municipal emergency response councils

[1628] The Government will strengthen emergency preparedness work in municipalities by requiring that municipalities have, or be affiliated with, a municipal emergency preparedness council

[1629] The government will ensure this through amendments to the Civil Protection Act

[1630] A requirement to “be affiliated” allows municipalities to collaborate on such a council

[1631] Which solution municipalities choose must be based on local assessments

[1632] The solution will provide sufficient flexibility for the municipalities' resource situation, uniqueness and opportunity for self-government, while at the same time volunteers and private businesses will be more closely integrated into the work on security and emergency preparedness

[1633] By setting requirements for municipal emergency preparedness councils, the government will ensure that the municipal emergency preparedness management has clear lines of responsibility, and at the same time facilitate a more unified council. [1671] Establish a reinforcement scheme for municipal crisis management

[1672] The government believes that municipalities that are severely affected by major incidents must receive the necessary rapid assistance from regional and national levels

[1673] In resource-intensive events that rarely occur, there may be a need to relieve the municipalities with expertise and capacity that it is not appropriate or possible to build up in each individual municipality

[1674] The Total Emergency Preparedness Commission recommended establishing a municipal reinforcement scheme that formalizes support from national and regional emergency response actors

[1675] These must be drawn upon request from the municipality

[1676] The commission pointed to resource needs that arise in all major crises related to psychosocial support, communication and coordination

[1677] The Government therefore believes that there is a need to review and systematize which resources, regionally and nationally, can be of assistance to municipalities affected by extraordinary events

[1678] The Government will therefore establish a reinforcement scheme for municipal crisis management

[1679] The resources in the reinforcement scheme must be tangible and available at short notice, and it should be clear who is included in it, where the resources are and what expertise they possess

[1680] Such a scheme would primarily represent a safety net for municipal emergency preparedness

[1681] Ordinary responsibilities and municipal self-government remain in place even if the municipality requests assistance to solve tasks

[1682] The Government will initiate work to specify the structure of the scheme, both with regard to which resources will be included, the interface to existing emergency preparedness schemes, and the roles and responsibilities of relevant actors

[2274] The project "1619 – BAS

[2275] Total Defence towards 2040" at the Norwegian Defence Research Institute is a research project in the period 2021–

[2276] It will prepare the necessary knowledge base for the long-term further development of total defence capability through R&D and the exploitation of technology, in support of long-term planning and policy formulation

[2277] The project has realized a number of partial deliveries in the form of published research products

[2278] The project's performance objectives are

[2279] – Contribute to increased understanding of how complex threats and societal developments in general can affect total defense capability

[2280] – Contribute to strengthening society's resilience through a functional-based approach to further develop total defense capabilities across the entire crisis spectrum

[2281] – Contribute to strengthening the ability to understand, analyze and manage complex threats across sectors to strengthen cross-sectoral situational awareness

[2282] – Promote proposals for alternative arrangements for the total defence capability in a 2040 perspective, both to strengthen Norway's security and to help support and enable future operational concepts for the Armed Forces

[2283] Project 1619 – BAS

[2284] Total Defence Towards 2040 is a further development of the Norwegian Defence Research Institute's research series on societal security and preparedness, the Protection of Society (BAS) series

[2285] The Norwegian Defence Research Institute started the series in the mid-1990s in collaboration with the Directorate for Civil Protection and Emergency Preparedness

[2286] The first BAS project was a mapping of critical societal functions that should be maintained during armed conflict and in peacetime

[2287] In the coming years, the Norwegian Defence Research Institute took a closer look at telecommunications preparedness, power preparedness, transport preparedness and ICT vulnerability

[2288] From 2007, BAS became more about civil-military cooperation and crisis management, and how major crises can and should be handled at the national level

[2289] Based on the BAS research and related research activities, the Norwegian Defence Research Institute has investigated the strengths and weaknesses of today's total defence for the Total Preparedness Commission

[2290] BAS research is still ongoing, and will in the future develop new knowledge that contributes to an active total defense that functions across the entire spectrum of conflicts and that strengthens Norwegian security and defense capabilities

[2369] A civil society that resists complex threats 2024–

[2370] Total preparedness report

[2371] Better ability to resist complex threats Foreign states use complex means that are broad-based, encompass both legal and illegal activities, last for a long time, and fall below the threshold of armed conflict

[2372] Threat actors may intend to target parts or all of society, to create discord between groups, to weaken trust and destabilize society, or to weaken preparedness and military capability in order to make the country more vulnerable

[2373] This type of use of instruments can be challenging to understand, detect, handle and counteract

[2374] The willingness and ability of threat actors to confront the West and Norway by using complex instruments appears to have increased

[2375] Composite measures affect the entire society

[2376] Both the defense sector and civilian sectors are affected, in the physical and digital space, and across areas of responsibility

[2377] Public bodies, private businesses and individuals can be exposed to such use of instruments

[2378] Actors who are affected may, for example, be linked to the delivery of critical goods and services such as power, petroleum products, electronic communications and water

[2379] In the long term, this activity could threaten our democracy, the rule of law, our social values, and Norway's economic and political space for action

[2380] This does not mean that we are at war, but the activity has consequences for how Norway – the population, municipalities, business and public administration – meets the challenges

[2381] At the same time, Norway has a toolbox of tools to address the threats

[2382] We can, at the state, societal and individual levels, contribute to strengthening society's resilience

[2383] Handling complex use of instruments requires information sharing across sectors, the ability to see events in context and a shared understanding of the situation

[2384] Strengthening society's resilience in peacetime acts as a deterrent and contributes to increased preparedness in times of crisis and armed conflict

[2385] A resilient population provides a better foundation for national security and defense capabilities

[2386] Large parts of the critical infrastructure in Norway are owned by private businesses

[2387] These actors have expertise in vulnerabilities and how incidents can best be handled within their own area of responsibility

[2388] They are a central part of our resilience and total defense

[2389] Close involvement of private actors in the work against complex threats is therefore important

[2412] Threats challenge society The war in Ukraine affects the intelligence, influence and sabotage threat in Norway

[2413] The Intelligence Service and the Police Security Service point out in their threat assessments that foreign states will use a broad range of instruments against and in Norway to achieve their goals

[2414] This applies particularly to authoritarian states

[2415] Among other things, it has been highlighted that the risk of sabotage against Norwegian weapons deliveries to Ukraine has increased

[2416] Fewer bilateral cooperation areas have led to Russia having reduced access to information about Norwegian affairs, and this requires more from Russian intelligence and security services than before

[2417] Russia will probably compensate for this by making greater use of visiting personnel, as well as substitutes, to carry out tasks previously carried out by permanently stationed intelligence personnel

[2418] Russian actors seek information about Norwegian politics, energy, the High North, allied activities and defense

[2419] Russia is also interested in Norwegian technology in areas they themselves have ambitions to develop

[2420] Russia uses civilian vessels in intelligence operations

[2421] They have legitimate access close to Norwegian infrastructure and the Norwegian coast

[2422] It can be challenging to uncover whether they are carrying out intelligence activities alongside their legal activities

[2423] China does not pose a direct military threat to Norway, but is interested in establishing a political and economic foothold in the Arctic and the independent ability to operate militarily in the region

[2424] Chinese directional services operate throughout Europe

[2425] The activity includes both intelligence activities and industrial espionage

[2426] The digital space is the most relevant gateway for the activity

[2427] Chinese diplomats, visiting delegations, private individuals, business actors and interest groups regularly carry out tasks on behalf of Chinese intelligence services

[2428] There are close links between Chinese intelligence services and Chinese commercial companies

[2429] Beijing has both the institutional resources and a legal framework to exploit Chinese businesses and Chinese individuals for state purposes

[2430] All Chinese companies and individuals are obligated by Chinese law to assist China's intelligence and security services

[2431] Collaboration with Chinese actors must be considered against this backdrop

[2469] against influence operations Influence operations are part of the composite threat picture

[2470] Influence operations refer to other states' use of overt and covert campaigns, operations and activities, often without the use of military force, to change attitudes, decisions or outcomes

[2471] The goal is often to influence political processes or decisions in a given direction, but can also be to reinforce polarization, spread mistrust or create general unrest among the population

[2472] Disinformation is one of several means to achieve this

[2473] Traditional media, alternative media and social media can be misused to spread disinformation, initiate smear campaigns, and spread rumors and half-truths

[2474] In Norway, some foreign intelligence officers will also work specifically against people who have political influence, in order to try to influence the outcome of individual cases

[2475] Attempts by foreign states to exert influence are described as a threat by both the Intelligence Service and the Police Security Service in the annual threat assessments

[2476] The Police Security Service believes that we must be prepared that Russian and Chinese intelligence services in particular will attempt to influence decision-makers and the population

[2477] For many years, Russia has demonstrated the ability and willingness to carry out influence operations in Western countries

[2484] Box 7.2 Amendments to the Criminal Code regarding influence from foreign intelligence

[2485] The Police Security Service is responsible for preventing and investigating serious crimes against national security

[2486] As part of this, the service will identify, assess and handle threats related to foreign states' use of instruments in Norway, there during influence operations

[2487] To provide the Police Security Service with an appropriate legal framework for this work, the Storting has adopted amendments to the Criminal Code

[2488] From 1 July 2024, two new provisions in the Criminal Code entered into force (sections 130 and 130 a

[2489] The provisions strengthen criminal law protection against harmful influence activities by foreign intelligence in Norway

[2490] The provisions make it a criminal offence to contribute on behalf of or in agreement with a foreign intelligence actor to activities that aim to influence decisions or the formation of public opinion, when the activities may harm significant societal interests

[2491] The Police Register Act allows the Police Security Service to store, systematize and analyze openly available information for policy purposes

[2492] Together with the above-mentioned amendments to the Criminal Code, this enables the Police Security Service to prepare analyses and assessments to provide decision-making support on issues that may threaten Norway's sovereignty, territorial integrity, democratic form of government and other national security interests

[2499] Actors with special responsibility in the work against influence

[2500] The principle of responsibility and the principle of cooperation are firmly established, and handling disinformation and influence is primarily the responsibility of the individual business and the sector affected

[2501] Certain ministries and agencies nevertheless have a special responsibility within various areas in the work against influence

[2502] – The Ministry of Justice and Public Security is responsible for general coordination of measures against influence operations on the civilian side, as well as professional responsibility for coordination and crisis management in situations where it is required

[2503] – The Ministry of Culture and Equality is responsible for strengthening the population's resistance to disinformation

[2504] – The Ministry of Defence is responsible for influence operations that are directed at the defence sector, defence policy and defence capabilities, or that may otherwise pose a military threat to national security, as well as international defence cooperation in the area

[2505] – The Ministry of Foreign Affairs is responsible for diplomatic, foreign policy and security policy aspects of disinformation and influence operations

[2506] – The Ministry of Local Government and District Affairs is responsible for the work against unwanted election influence

[2507] Agencies – The police are responsible for complex substance use that materializes as crime, and must handle and restore normalcy, while also conducting research

[2562] Total preparedness report National control

[2563] The Government will strengthen national control and increase the level of knowledge in society about risk, threat actors and preventive security work

[2564] National control is an important tool for safeguarding national security

[2565] National control over businesses, infrastructure, natural resources, property and assets that are important for national security can be achieved through instruments such as regulations, various forms of ownership, oversight, cooperation and advice and guidance

[2566] National control as a tool must be used in a way that contributes to predictability and trust

[2567] The Government will contribute to ensuring that businesses subject to the Security Act, the business community, municipalities and county councils are able to make good assessments to safeguard national security

[2568] • ensure sufficient national control over property that has security significance, critical infrastructure, natural resources and strategically important companies and value chains

[2569] • increase control of property for reasons of national security by investigating mandatory ownership registration to achieve sufficient overview of, and control over, ownership of real estate

[2570] • propose necessary regulatory changes that ensure an approval mechanism for the purchase of certain properties

[2571] • propose a new law for the control of foreign investments that will help safeguard national security interests and ensure that Norway remains an attractive country for foreign investments

[2572] • propose changes to the data center regulations to ensure the authorities' ability to prevent, deter, stop and investigate crime and handle the loss of data center services that are important to society

[2573] • ensure that national security is safeguarded in new regulations and revisions of existing ones where relevant

[2574] • strengthen security in the maritime sector and ensure that there is close cooperation and coordination between civil and military authorities, as well as between the private and public sectors

[2576] Trade-offs between transparency, business interests and national security

[3125] The border with Russia

[3126] The national border between Norway and Russia is 197.7 km long, and two-thirds of it runs through the Pasvik River

[3127] Since 1959, the Norwegian Armed Forces have had the task of maintaining border security on the Norwegian-Russian border

[3128] The Garrison in Sør-Varanger (GSV) carries out the task on behalf of and in collaboration with the police

[3129] Cooperation with the Armed Forces is stipulated in the Border Act

[3130] The national border can only be crossed at the Storskog border crossing point

[3131] Valid travel documents are required

[3132] The Border Guard actively conducts preventive information work with its own patrols, and the area is under continuous surveillance

[3133] The Border Guard has police authority and is present on behalf of the police to provide information and implement preventive measures against violations of the law in border areas and waterways

[3134] It also means that Border Guard personnel can issue orders if they uncover movement and behavior that may lead to violations of the law

[3135] The police have national responsibility for the Schengen external border and person control at the Storskog border crossing point

[3161] Applicable and future-oriented emergency legislation is a necessary prerequisite for effective crisis management, and is fundamental for both emergency planning and training

[3165] Other emergency powers, such as the powers in the Food and Drug Emergency Preparedness Act, the Requisition Act, the Civil Protection Act, the Health Emergency Preparedness Act and the other power provisions in the Infection Control Act, are in turn important examples of ordinary emergency powers

[3202] Box 10.4 International law of war

[3203] The international law of war refers to a part of international law that applies in armed conflict and is not intended to prohibit war, but to regulate the conduct of warfare

[3204] The rules in this part of international law have been developed in a balance between considerations of military necessity on the one hand, and humanitarian considerations on the other

[3205] Provisions aimed at protecting civilians from the consequences of the fighting are therefore central

[3206] According to Articles 51 and 52 of the First Additional Protocol to the Geneva Conventions, civilians and civilian objects shall not be made the object of attack

[3207] Civilians may nevertheless lose their protected status if they take a direct part in hostilities, see Additional Protocol I, Article

[3208] Persons who are not lawful targets, for example civilians and objects, shall be protected from attack

[3209] Even if protected persons are not directly attacked, in many cases they will still fall victim to the effects of attacks on lawful targets, for example if they are in the vicinity of a lawful military objective

[3210] Under the international law of war, civilian casualties in an attack can be accepted if there is proportionality between the expected concrete and direct military advantage on the one hand, and the risk of civilian casualties on the other

[3211] The parties to the conflict must also exercise continuous care to spare civilians during the conduct of military operations, see Additional Protocol I, Article

[3212] This means that the risk of collateral damage to civilians must be managed and kept as low as possible

[3402] The government proposes to develop a strategic corridor for military mobility through northern Norway, northern Sweden and northern Finland

[3403] The measure will have significant economic consequences

[3404] The three countries must identify bottlenecks and consider updating regulations and plans before any concrete investment needs can be stated

[3405] The planning itself will not have significant economic or administrative consequences

[3406] Implementation of the NIS2 Directive and the CER Directive The government is preparing the implementation of the NIS2 Directive and the CER Directive in Norwegian law

[3407] The directives set, among other things, basic requirements for safety, notification and routines

[3408] When the directives are incorporated into Norwegian law, it could have financial and administrative consequences for businesses that are covered

[3409] The directives affect several sectors, and for businesses that are not currently subject to similar safety requirements, it is assumed that the economic and administrative consequences may be of a certain magnitude

[3410] The Ministry of Justice and Public Security will further investigate the financial and administrative consequences in connection with the legislative work

[3411] The government wants the Storting to repeal the decision from 1998 to temporarily halt construction of shelters in new buildings

[3412] The proposal entails significant economic and administrative consequences that have the potential to affect many administrative units, including the municipal sector and businesses in the business sector

[3413] The measure will also require budgetary funds in the state budget

[3414] The Directorate for Civil Protection and Emergency Preparedness has made some preliminary estimates of the costs associated with establishing shelters and refuges in new buildings

[3415] They will vary between different buildings and how the building itself is planned to be built, for example whether the building is planned to have underground areas or not

[3416] The Directorate estimates an additional cost for the developer of 30,000 NOK per shelter space and annual maintenance costs of 85 NOK per space

[3417] For covered spaces, the directorate has calculated an additional cost for the developer of 6,000–10,000 NOK per covered space and virtually no annual maintenance costs

[3418] The Ministry will specify the financial and administrative consequences in connection with the regulatory work and public consultation on the matter

[3419] The Government will strengthen the civil defence's ability to meet the new challenges by increasing the target number of conscripts from 8,000 to

[3420] The ceiling entails an annual increase in appropriations in the state budget of approximately NOK 87 million, and triggers a one-time investment requirement of NOK 30 million at the Civil Defence Competence Centre

[3421] Administrative considerations indicate that the proposal will be implemented over a period of approximately eight years

[3422] The Directorate for Civil Protection and Emergency Preparedness will prepare an implementation strategy

[3423] The measure also entails an opportunity cost equal to production and leisure time lost in training and effort for new conscripts

[3424] Strengthening civil defense could also have administrative and financial consequences for municipalities, which, under the Civil Protection Act, are responsible for storing civil defense equipment

[3425] Volunteers A financial escalation plan for increased subsidies to voluntary organizations of up to NOK 100 million will have financial consequences

[3426] How large this will be depends on the speed of escalation and must be clarified through the ordinary budget processes
